column4: The ayah names ذكر الله and إقامة الصلاة among acts from which trade does not distract these men; it sets remembrance and prayer inside ordinary work.

This is the worship-house setting just before 24:37: God's name is mentioned and He is glorified morning and evening. The next ayah adds remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving among men not distracted by commerce.
Musa is told أقم الصلاة لذكري, making remembrance the stated purpose of prayer, just as the section joins the two acts.
In Musa's request that Harun share his task, the purpose كي نسبحك كثيرا is collective glorification; the section likewise treats tasbih as part of a shared devotional practice.
The same request continues with ونذكرك كثيرا: Musa pairs frequent remembrance with the glorification in 20:33, directly echoing the section's linked verbs.
At the Friday call to prayer, believers are told to hasten to ذكر الله and leave trade; this gives the section's remembrance-and-prayer pairing a concrete public setting.
After prayer, the ayah permits dispersal for livelihood and commands abundant remembrance; it makes explicit the continuation of worship into ordinary activity.
The ayah joins Quran recitation to prayer, says prayer restrains wrongdoing, and calls ذكر الله أكبر. That cognate of the section's كبرى for the fire assigns greatness to remembrance instead.
The ayah says every creature knows its صلاة and تسبيح. It extends the section's creaturely prayer and broad tasbih definitions beyond human bodily worship.
Believers are commanded to remember Allah with much remembrance, matching the section's dictionary sense of dhikr as something repeatedly running on the tongue.
The adjoining command to glorify Allah morning and evening pairs tasbih with 33:41's remembrance, the same linked practice and daily rhythm developed in the section.

Here Allah يصلي عليكم to bring believers from darkness into light. This is the divine-side sense named in the section, where Allah's salat is described as purification, rather than a person's ritual prayer.

The Prophet is told صل عليهم after charity that purifies its givers; their prayer is called reassurance. This joins the section's two directions, purification and a human salat that includes supplication.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord before sunrise and sunset and at night; it is a direct counterpart to the section's opening imperative and its timed worship scenes.

This ayah's own contribution is the crowd leaving the Messenger standing for trade and amusement, reversing the undistracted men of 24:37; 62:9-10 supply the preceding Friday prayer and remembrance commands.
The command ولا تجهر بصلاتك ولا تخافت بها gives a precise boundary for audible prayer. It activates the section's dictionary entry for جهر as making speech, prayer, and recitation audible.
After prayer, believers are told to remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on their sides; it connects salat and dhikr while showing remembrance continues beyond the bodily prayer.
The Prophet is told واذكر اسم ربك and to devote himself wholly to God, directly meeting the section's mention of the Lord's name and remembrance.

This long instruction puts Quran recitation, إقامة الصلاة, giving, and seeking forgiveness together; it concretely supports the section's claim that recitation and prayer belong to one devotional practice.
The command واذكر اسم ربك بكرة وأصيلا repeats the section's remembrance of the Lord's name and gives it a morning-evening rhythm.
The ayah adds night prostration and lengthy glorification after 76:25's remembrance command, making bodily prayer and tasbih parts of one daily pattern.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord before sunrise and sunset, a direct version of the section's opening command to glorify the Lord's name.
The command continues with night glorification and أدبار السجود, explicitly bringing tasbih together with prostration, one of the bodily acts in the section's salat definition.
After distress at what people say, the Prophet is told to glorify his Lord with praise and be among those prostrating; this joins verbal praise with the bodily prayer named in the section.
Those reminded by God's signs fall prostrate, glorify their Lord with praise, and are not arrogant; the ayah stages reminder, sujud, and tasbih as one response.
Believers are told to bow, prostrate, worship their Lord, and do good so that they may prosper. This gives concrete bodily content to the section's account of salat and links it to success.

The battle prayer divides worshippers into groups, with one group prostrating while another stands guard. The section's dictionary defines creaturely salat through bodily acts including standing and prostration.
The command to guard the prayers and stand قانتين makes the standing posture explicit, matching the section's bodily definition of salat.
This command joins establishing prayer and giving zakat with bowing among those who bow, a concrete bodily act in the section's definition of human salat.
Zakariya is standing in prayer in the sanctuary when the angels call to him; the verse shows the bodily stance included in the section's definition of salat.

Abraham asks to be made one who establishes الصلاة, then separately asks that his دعاء be accepted. The section's dictionary also lists supplication as a sense within salat; this verse clarifies the neighboring uses.
Those near their Lord do not disdain worship, glorify Him, and prostrate to Him; the verse directly combines the section's broad tasbih sense with a bodily act of prayer.

The faithful invoke their Lord morning and evening, while the warning is not to prefer worldly adornment or follow one heedless of ذكر الله. It reverses the section's undistracted remembrance amid trade.
The ayah condemns those who bar God's name from being mentioned in mosques and seek their ruin; it reverses the worship-house scene of 24:36, where the name is remembered and God glorified.
After a person forbids a servant's prayer, the command is كلا لا تطعه واسجد واقترب: prostration is the bodily approach that answers the attempted interruption of worship.
The direct command فسبح باسم ربك العظيم closely matches 87:1's command to glorify the name of the Lord Most High.
The surah closes with the same command to glorify the name of the Lord Most Great, a second direct Quranic formulation of the section's opening act.
After defending the Quran as revelation, the ayah ends فسبح باسم ربك العظيم, again pairing glorification with the Lord's name as in 87:1.
The near-verbatim claim قد أفلح من زكاها links success with purification, the two ideas joined in 87:14 just before the prayer the section discusses.
This person gives wealth to purify himself; it parallels 87:14's successful purification while showing a distinct act through which purification is pursued.
The most God-fearing person is spared the blazing fire, joining fear and escape from punishment as in 87:10-12, before the next ayah describes purification.
Musa asks Pharaoh هل لك إلى أن تزكى, a direct call to purification that echoes 87:14 and gives the section's tazkiya link a prophetic scene.
Musa continues by offering to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he may fear Him; this joins guidance and fear as 87:3 and 87:10 do around the section's worship image.
The warning فلا تزكوا أنفسكم reverses 87:14's successful purification: the passage says God knows best who is truly mindful, clarifying that purification is not self-congratulation.
The Quran is called a تذكرة, directly supporting the section's dictionary treatment of Quran recitation as remembrance.
The next ayah says فمن شاء ذكره: whoever wills may remember it, linking Quranic reminder with the remembering person in 87:10.
The passage concludes that they remember only if God wills, a specific parallel to 87:6-7's recitation, forgetting, and divine will.
The Quran is called a تذكرة, a direct match for the section's dictionary sense that reciting Quran is dhikr.
The following ayah says فمن شاء ذكره; it describes the response to Quranic reminder that the section connects to the one who remembers.
After the account of Noah's people, this ayah says the Quran is made easy for remembrance; it explicitly joins recitation and dhikr as the section's dictionary does.
After the account of Aad, the repeated claim that the Quran is easy for remembrance again names recitation as dhikr.
After Thamud's destruction, the refrain that the Quran is easy for remembrance makes Quranic recitation the response to a warning.
After the account of Lot's people, the same Quran-for-remembrance refrain confirms this connection across repeated warnings.
The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hastily while receiving revelation; this directly recalls 87:6's promised recitation and the section's link between recitation and remembrance.
The ayah says collecting and reciting the revelation are God's responsibility, illuminating the section's statement that God will make the Prophet recite.
The Prophet is instructed to follow the Quran when it is recited, specifying the responsive act behind the section's Quran-recitation-as-dhikr gloss.
The passage concludes that explaining the recitation is God's responsibility, completing the revelation sequence that 87:6 summarizes.
The Quran was sent as a reminder for one who fears; this directly joins recitation and fear, the two responses linked in 87:6 and 87:10.
When the Quran is recited, listeners are told to listen and be quiet for mercy; it makes the section's recitation-as-remembrance a shared act of hearing.
The ayah says the Prophet was not taught poetry but that the message is ذكر and a clear Quran, directly naming Quran as remembrance.
The Quran is invoked as ذي الذكر, a direct formulation of the section's dictionary claim that Quran recitation is dhikr.
The revealed scripture is called a blessed ذكر, linking the section's recitation to a transmitted reminder.
The revelation is called a ذكر for the Prophet and his people, a direct lexical counterpart to the section's account of Quran recitation as remembrance.
The ayah calls the revelation الذكر and promises its preservation; alongside 87:6's promise that the Prophet will not forget, it presents divine keeping of the reminder.
Those who recite God's book and establish prayer hope for a trade that will not fail; it joins Quran recitation to prayer and recasts the commerce that cannot distract the men of 24:37.
The Quran is divided so the Prophet may recite it to people over time; this gives a concrete public form to the section's claim that Quran reading is remembrance.
A group of jinn listens to the Quran being recited and then returns to warn its people, showing recitation becoming remembrance shared with others.
Remember Me; I will remember you, and be grateful to Me. The ayah directly connects dhikr with gratitude, another sense listed in the section's dictionary entry.
Zakariya signals to his people to glorify God morning and evening; this depicts tasbih as enacted communication and a repeated daily practice.
Zakariya is told to remember his Lord much and glorify Him morning and evening, combining the section's linked roots in a single prophetic instruction.
The command glorifies God at evening and morning, a direct daily-rhythm counterpart to tasbih in the section and its 24:36 parallel.
This ayah assigns praise to God and repeats evening, afternoon, and noon times; it supplies the praise-and-time frame around 30:17's glorification, while its own contribution is praise.
Hypocrites stand for prayer lazily, show off, and remember God only a little; this directly reverses the section's remembrance and prayer as one attentive practice.
This ayah names intoxicants, gambling, altars, and divining arrows as things to avoid; 5:91 explains their specific effect of diverting people from remembrance and prayer.
The ayah says Satan uses intoxicants and gambling to turn people away from ذكر الله and الصلاة, naming the very pair the section joins and showing a force that breaks their practice apart.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from ذكر الله, and those who do are called losers; this echoes the commerce that fails to distract the men in 24:37.
The command وذكر فإن الذكرى تنفع المؤمنين closely matches 87:9's charge to remind if the reminder benefits, naming the same work and its effect.
The instruction واذكر ربك إذا نسيت directly connects remembrance of the Lord with forgetting, clarifying the section's reading of 87:6-7.
Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned are described as patient, establishing prayer, and giving; it joins dhikr and salat in a lived response.
The Messenger recites God's verses to people and purifies them before teaching the Book; this joins recitation and tazkiya, the two actions the section connects across 87:14-15.
The Messenger recites God's verses, purifies the believers, and teaches them the Book and wisdom; this directly joins recitation and purification as the section does across 87:14-15.
The Messenger recites verses, purifies believers, and teaches them the Book and wisdom; it makes the section's Quran-recitation and purification link explicit.
The command to establish prayer is followed by Quran recitation at dawn, where the recitation is witnessed; the ayah directly puts salat and recitation together at appointed times.
The Prophet is told to keep a night vigil as an additional devotion; it supplies a specific bodily prayer practice within the section's account of salat.
The Prophet is told to glorify his Lord with praise morning and evening after being told to be patient; it directly joins tasbih, praise, and a daily rhythm.
The Prophet is told to be patient and glorify his Lord with praise when he rises; it connects glorification and praise to the section's devotional command.
The instruction to glorify God at night and as stars set extends the preceding command into night worship, echoing the section's body-and-remembrance rhythm.
Those questioned about entering Saqar answer that they were not among the people who prayed; this makes prayer's absence a direct contrast to the successful worshipper in 87:14-15.
The gardens are the reward of one who purifies himself; this links the section's tazkiya bridge between 87:14 and 87:15 to an explicit promised outcome.
The ayah describes a mosque where the Prophet is to stand and men who love purification; it directly meets the section's bodily prayer and salat-as-tazkiya strands.
The people of Paradise begin their دعوى with سبحانك اللهم and end it with الحمد لله; this directly gathers tasbih, supplication, and praise, which the section's dictionary lists under dhikr.
The verse says that if the Prophet speaks aloud, God knows what is secret and more hidden; this closely mirrors 87:7's knowledge of الجهر and what is hidden.
God is said to know your secret and your public speech; the exact جهر/secrecy opposition echoes 87:7's known public and hidden speech.
The Prophet is told to remind by the Quran those who fear God's warning, joining Quranic recitation, reminder, and fear as 87:9-10 do.
The command فذكر إنما أنت مذكر directly parallels 87:9's instruction to remind and identifies the Prophet's role as reminder.
Whoever turns away from God's remembrance is promised a constricted life and blindness on the Day of Resurrection, a direct reversal of 87:10's remembering person who fears.
The passage describes one who turns away from God's remembrance and wants only worldly life, directly meeting 87:11 and the later contrast with worldly preference.
Whoever is blinded from remembrance of the Merciful is assigned a devil as companion; it gives a specific consequence to the avoidance in 87:11.
The Prophet must not dismiss those who call on their Lord morning and evening for His face or follow the heedless; this parallels the section's regular worship and warning against distraction.
Satan is said to make people forget remembrance of Allah; this gives the section's forgetting motif a direct contrary case.
The phrase الجهر بالسوء من القول uses the section's root ج ه ر for public speech, though its context concerns public evil words rather than audible prayer.
Believers are told to seek help through patience and prayer, which is difficult except for the humble who expect to meet their Lord; this connects salat to the section's humility and fear.
The passage asks about those who claim purity and answers that Allah purifies whom He wills, a direct contrast to treating 87:14's tazkiya as self-congratulation.
The ayah says no one would be purified without God's favor, but Allah purifies whom He wills; it develops the divine-side purification linked to salat in the section.
The patient receive صلوات from their Lord and mercy. This is a divine-side use of the salat root, though whether it carries the section's specific sense of purification here is uncertain.
Allah and the angels يصلون على النبي and believers are told to do so too; it displays the non-ritual salat sense named in the section, though the verse addresses the Prophet specifically.
The verse contrasts one who conceals speech with one who proclaims it; this matches the section's public/private wording around الجهر, though the speech here is not specifically prayer.
The ayah allows believers to conceal or proclaim their speech and says God knows what is in their hearts, a close verbal parallel to 87:7's known public and hidden speech.
All creation glorifies God with praise, extending the section's dictionary definition of tasbih as worship beyond spoken human praise; the verse itself is about creation's response.
These believers remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, postures that overlap the section's bodily account of prayer while showing remembrance continuing through ordinary positions.
When God is mentioned, believers' hearts tremble, and recited signs increase their faith; it gives the section's remembrance and recitation a specific inward response.
The verse says hearts find rest in remembrance of God, a specific effect of dhikr that complements the section's account of remembering as an act.
When the Merciful's signs are recited, earlier prophets fall prostrate and weep; this joins recitation to bodily submission as the section joins reminder and prayer.
When Quran is recited to people given knowledge, they fall prostrate; this directly stages the section's recitation and bodily salat together.
Their prostration is followed by declaring their Lord's promise true and praising Him; the response moves from bodily prayer to verbal praise.
The passage closes with weeping prostration and increased humility, specifying the inward result of the recitation scene begun in 17:107.
The servants of the Merciful spend nights prostrating and standing, a clear scene of the bodily acts that the section lists within salat.
The devoted person stands and prostrates through the night, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for mercy; it brings the section's bodily prayer together with its one-who-fears motif.
Mary is told to prostrate and bow with those who bow; the verse supplies the bodily gestures that the section's dictionary gives for prayer.
The believers bear a sign on their faces from prostration, making the section's bodily prayer image visible in the body.
When told to prostrate to the Merciful, the deniers ask who He is and turn away; it is a specific refusal of the bodily worship that the section includes in salat.
The first command to recite is اقرأ باسم ربك, joining Quran reading to the Lord's name as the section joins remembrance with the Lord's name.
The passage asks about one who forbids a servant's prayer; it introduces a concrete obstruction to the bodily worship that the section describes.
This ayah specifies that the forbidden act is a servant's prayer, sharpening the contrast between interruption and the section's act of salat.
This verse directs woe at those identified as praying; 107:5 names their fault as heedlessness, so the passage distinguishes the rite from mindful remembrance.
This ayah asks what brought people into Saqar; 74:43 gives their answer, that they were not among those who prayed. Its own contribution is to frame the fire as a question of conduct.
These worshippers are heedless of their prayers; the section explicitly reads this as a form of forgetting, a reversal of its remember-and-pray closing act.
This ayah adds that they act to be seen, extending 107:4-5's warning about heedless prayer into ostentation; its contribution is the motive behind the neglect.
The final ayah adds that they withhold even small aid, completing the passage's reversal of the section's prayer as an active practice of obedience.
The soul's failure is its corruption, the reverse of 91:9's successful purification and 87:14's person who purifies himself.
Pharaoh claims أنا ربكم الأعلى, reversing 87:1's command to glorify the Lord Most High by making himself the highest lord.
This ayah says the reminder's bearer is not a controller over the people; 88:21 gives his task to remind and 88:23 describes those who turn away, so this verse sets the limit of the role.
This ayah's own contribution is the person who turns away and disbelieves; 88:21 names the reminder he rejects, paralleling the avoidance in 87:11.

The one who turns away and disbelieves is threatened with the greatest punishment, joining rejection of reminder to punishment as in 87:11-12; الأكبر also recalls the section's comparison with أكبر in 29:45.
